items.definition: Keeping the account but changing the words in it, until the meaning that was shared is gone.
items.example: The word was changed from late to careless, and that was revisionism.

items.definition: The doubt a person is given about their own memory, until they check themselves instead of the facts.
items.example: The result was manufactured doubt: he began to check his own memory instead of the record.

items.definition: The name of the pattern of three moves: deny, attack, and reverse victim and offender.
items.example: The pattern was DARVO: deny, attack, and reverse victim and offender.

items.definition: The refusal to accept a shared account, said in a way that does not change when the evidence appears.
items.example: The denial was said the same way every time, and the message did not change it.

items.definition: The move that turns on the person who holds the account, so that the person becomes the problem.
items.example: The attack moved the talk from the handover to her tone.

items.definition: The move that puts the two sides in the wrong places, crediting the harm to the person who suffered it.
items.example: The reversal put the person who caused the harm in the place of the person who suffered it.

items.definition: Turning a question back on the person who asked it, so that the original question is never answered.
items.example: The deflection worked once, and I still had not answered what was wrong with the drawing.

items.definition: Putting your own act on the other person, and calling it the other person's character.
items.example: It was projection: the person who had been aggressive called the other one aggressive.

items.definition: Bringing a third person into a dispute between two, so that the two cannot settle it themselves.
items.example: Triangulation brought a third person into a dispute between two people.

items.definition: The written record that keeps a shared account alive when memory is attacked.
items.example: The documentation was a handover note, a date and a message.

items.definition: The small set of fixed sentences used to rewrite an account, at work and at home.
items.example: The gaslighting vocabulary is short: you are misremembering, I never said that.

items.definition: The ability to make things happen, whether or not the people affected agree.
items.example: The power to shut the line down was in his hands, and it did not need anybody's permission.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that puts the decision in the hands of an expert, real or claimed.
items.example: It used authority: the technician said the part was safe, and showed no manual.

items.definition: Authority whose basis can be named and questioned, such as checked knowledge, a defined role or a rule that applies to everybody.
items.example: It was legitimate authority: she showed the standard and said who had signed the rule.

items.definition: Power that belongs to an office or an organisation rather than to a person, and passes on with the role.
items.example: Institutional power is why the badge opens the door even though the badge is not the man.

items.definition: The pressure to return a favour that the other side has given you.
items.example: The discount was the favour, and the renewal at the same price was the bill.

items.definition: The habit of giving way to authority without asking for the reason.
items.example: Deference is not weakness, but a room full of deference has nobody left to check anything.

items.definition: Any effect one person has on another, from a request to advice, in either direction.
items.example: Influence is not a privilege: the newest member of the team influences the oldest one as well.

items.definition: An honest attempt to win agreement, in which the other person is free to say no.
items.example: That was persuasion, not pressure: he explained the plan and left the decision to her.

items.definition: The removal of a real choice by force or by the threat of harm.
items.example: Sign the form today or lose the job — that is coercion, not persuasion.

items.definition: The arrangement of roles that says who decides and who answers for the decision.
items.example: The hierarchy is clear on paper; the account, the invoice and the parts were not.

items.definition: The formal authority to act, together with the limits that bound it.
items.example: His mandate was to negotiate the price, not to sign the contract.

items.definition: The condition that the reasons for a decision are visible and can be checked by the people affected.
items.example: Transparency was missing: nobody could say which number the decision was based on.

items.definition: The rules a decision must follow: notice, the chance to be heard, a written reason and a way to appeal.
items.example: Without due process the decision was final, and there was nowhere to take it.

items.definition: The answer you owe for an act, to the people affected and to the law.
items.example: The mistake was hers, and the accountability was hers as well.

items.definition: An AI system that plans and acts toward a goal, using tools and intermediate steps rather than answering in one shot.
A setup in which several specialized AI agents divide a task among themselves and pass work along.
The coordination of multiple agents: deciding their roles, order, tools and stopping conditions.
A design in which a person reviews and approves an agent's work before it takes effect.
The process of checking that output meets its requirements before it is used or shipped.
Assigning a task and the authority to complete it; with agents, the responsibility still stays with the delegator.
An AI assistant integrated into the development process that writes, completes and explains code on request.
The automatic production of program code from a natural-language description or an example.
Breaking a large, vague problem into small, precise, solvable parts with clear success conditions.
Reasoning about how the parts of a system affect each other, including effects that appear far away in time or structure.
The capacity to make good technical decisions under uncertainty, weighing trade-offs that no rule can settle.
The ongoing work of keeping software alive: fixing, adapting, and explaining it across years of changing conditions.
Software designed to act toward goals with a degree of autonomy rather than waiting for each command.
A user interface that changes according to context, intent and history rather than showing fixed menus.
A statement of what the user wants to achieve, as opposed to the commands that achieve it.
